title: The Completion Accounts Clause: The Reason Your Sale Price Can Still Move After You've Signed
excerpt: The headline price gets agreed, the contract gets signed, and months later a reconciliation clause can still move the final number. Here is what a completion accounts adjustment actually does.
content:
The sale price gets agreed after months of negotiation. Due diligence is done, the heads of terms are signed, and the number has been said out loud enough times that it starts to feel real. Then the business and asset sale agreement lands on the desk, and buried in the clauses nobody reads twice is a mechanism that can move that number by six figures after settlement has already happened.

It is called a completion accounts adjustment, sometimes a working capital peg, and it exists in some form in most SME sale agreements whether the seller clocked it at signing or not. The price agreed on the front page assumes the business will hold a certain level of working capital, debtors less payables, stock on hand, accrued leave, at the moment ownership actually changes hands. What gets banked on settlement day is provisional. What gets banked for good is decided later, once the real completion date figures are prepared and compared against that assumed target.

The pattern we typically see across owner-led businesses on the East Coast is that this clause gets almost no attention during negotiation, because the headline multiple and the purchase price are where all the emotional energy goes. Then two or three months after settlement, a reconciliation lands that reduces the final payment, and it feels like losing money on a deal that was supposedly already done.

Why the Number on Settlement Day Isn't the Final Number

Working capital is harder to pin down than a headline multiple, because it moves daily. A buyer agreeing to pay for a business today, based on financials from three months ago, needs some way of confirming that the working capital they are actually taking on at handover matches what was assumed in the price. The completion accounts mechanism solves that by setting a target, often the trailing twelve month average, and then adjusting the final price against the actual position on completion day, dollar for dollar in either direction.

This isn't a trick clause or a sign of a buyer acting in bad faith. It is a standard mechanism built to protect both sides from the gap between the financials used to set the business valuation and the actual state of the business on the day ownership changes. The issue for most sellers isn't the mechanism itself. It is that nobody explained it clearly enough, early enough, for it to influence how the business was run in the lead up to completion.

What Actually Moves the Final Figure

The completion accounts are usually prepared by the buyer's accountants within sixty to ninety days of settlement, with the seller given a right to review and query the figures before they are locked in. What moves the number is rarely dramatic. A batch of aged debtors gets written down once the new owner starts chasing them properly. A stock count on the actual completion date comes in lower than the estimate used at signing. Accrued leave or superannuation that was always owing gets picked up in full for the first time in the handover accounts.

None of this reflects anyone doing the wrong thing. A bookkeeper maintaining accurate monthly figures for compliance purposes is doing exactly what that function is meant to do. Completion accounts ask a different question, whether the working capital position on one specific contractual date matches a number negotiated months earlier, and that is a commercial read that sits above the compliance ledger rather than a gap in it.

Protecting the Number Before the Negotiation Starts

The sellers who come out of this process closest to the number they expected are the ones who treat working capital as something to manage deliberately in the run up to a sale, not just report on. Debtors get chased on normal terms rather than left to run long because a sale is in progress. Stock gets right sized rather than built up. Accruals get recorded properly well before anyone is reconciling against them.

A vendor due diligence pack prepared ahead of going to market does the same job from the other direction, getting the debtor book, work in progress and accrued liabilities genuinely clean and documented before a buyer ever sets a peg against them. It protects the number that was actually agreed, rather than leaving it exposed to a reconciliation nobody saw coming. Getting this right starts well before a letter of intent is on the table, which is exactly why an exit readiness diagnostic is worth running years, not months, ahead of a planned sale. If a sale is somewhere on your horizon, booking a discovery call early is what gives this mechanism time to work in your favour instead of against you.

faqs.q: What is a completion accounts adjustment in an Australian business sale?
faqs.a: It is the mechanism that trues up the final sale price against the actual working capital, debtors, stock and accrued liabilities, measured on the completion date rather than the figures used when the price was first agreed. Most Australian SME sale agreements include some version of it, and it can move the final proceeds up or down from the headline number signed on the contract.

faqs.q: Why can the sale price still change after settlement day in an SME sale?
faqs.a: Settlement is when ownership and funds change hands, but it usually isn't the final word on price. Most sale agreements set a working capital target the business is assumed to hold at completion, then compare that target against the real figures once completion accounts are prepared afterwards. The gap between the two, in either direction, adjusts what the seller actually ends up being paid.

faqs.q: How is the working capital target or peg usually set in a sale agreement?
faqs.a: It is typically calculated from a trailing average, often the last twelve months of the business's normal working capital position, debtors and stock less payables and accruals. Both parties negotiate this figure before signing, and it becomes the benchmark the actual completion date numbers are measured against once completion accounts are finalised.

faqs.q: What typically causes a completion accounts figure to come in lower than expected?
faqs.a: Usually a handful of unglamorous items rather than one dramatic discovery. Aged debtors written down once a new owner starts chasing them, a stock count that comes in under the estimate used at signing, or accrued leave and superannuation picked up in full for the first time in the handover accounts. None of it is unusual, which is exactly why it catches unprepared sellers off guard.

faqs.q: Can a seller dispute the completion accounts calculation after settlement?
faqs.a: Yes, most sale agreements give the seller a defined window to review and query the figures before they are locked in. Disputed items are often resolved with input from an independent accountant or a formal business valuation process, which is one reason the underlying numbers are worth getting right well before that stage is ever reached.

faqs.q: How long after settlement are completion accounts usually finalised in Australia?
faqs.a: Most sale agreements allow sixty to ninety days for the buyer to prepare completion accounts, plus a further review period for the seller to raise queries. It is common for the final adjustment, and the final cheque, to land three to four months after settlement day rather than on the day itself.

faqs.q: How can an Australian SME owner protect their sale price before signing a sale agreement?
faqs.a: The strongest protection is managing working capital deliberately in the run up to a sale rather than only reporting on it, so debtors, stock and accruals are already clean when a peg gets negotiated. Getting a vendor due diligence pack prepared ahead of going to market does this groundwork early, before a buyer ever sets the benchmark the final price gets measured against.
